```diff
+ # -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
+ """Generate 09_bme_categorical.ipynb"""
+ import nbformat as nbf
+ 
+ nb = nbf.v4.new_notebook()
+ nb.metadata['kernelspec'] = {'display_name': 'Python 3', 'language': 'python', 'name': 'python3'}
+ nb.metadata['language_info'] = {'name': 'python', 'version': '3.9.0'}
+ cells = []
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 0 – Title &amp; learning objectives
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "# Tutorial 09 – BME for Categorical Data\n\n"
+ "**Package:** stamps_v3  \n"
+ "**MATLAB equivalent:** &#96;BMEPROBALIBtutorial.m&#96; (categorical section) + &#96;STATLIBtutorial.m&#96;  \n"
+ "**Dataset:** Falmagne soil dataset – 118 georeferenced soil samples, Dinant area, Belgium\n\n"
+ "---\n\n"
+ "## Learning objectives\n\n"
+ "By the end of this notebook you will be able to:\n\n"
+ "1. **Represent** categorical observations as one-hot soft-data PDFs.\n"
+ "2. **Compute** empirical bivariate probability tables with &#96;probatablecalc&#96;.\n"
+ "3. **Fit** a smooth probability model (kernel regression) with &#96;probatablefit&#96;.\n"
+ "4. **Map** soil types over a regular grid using three estimators:\n"
+ "   - **BMEcatPdf** – full Maximum Entropy BME (most rigorous, slowest).\n"
+ "   - **MCPcatPdf** – Maximum Conditional Probability fast approximation.\n"
+ "   - **HBMEcatPdf** – Hybrid BME: MCP regional prior + local BME update.\n"
+ "5. **Validate** each method with Leave-One-Out cross-validation (LOOCV).\n"
+ "6. **Interpret** posterior category probability maps.\n\n"
+ "---\n\n"
+ "## Background: categorical BME in a nutshell\n\n"
+ "Categorical BME (Christakos &amp; Li, 1998) extends classical BME to discrete\n"
+ "variables. Instead of a Gaussian covariance model, spatial dependence is\n"
+ "encoded by a **bivariate probability table** $P(X_i = c_1, X_j = c_2 \\mid h)$\n"
+ "that gives the joint probability of observing two categories at two locations\n"
+ "separated by lag $h$.\n\n"
+ "The **Maximum Entropy** principle integrates this prior dependence structure\n"
+ "with the observed data (hard or soft) to produce a **posterior marginal PDF**\n"
+ "$P(X_k = c \\mid \\text{data})$ at each estimation point $k$.  The MAP\n"
+ "(most probable category) is then taken as the point estimate.\n\n"
+ "### Workflow at a glance\n\n"
+ "&#96;&#96;&#96;\n"
+ "Observations (soil codes 1–4)\n"
+ "      │\n"
+ "      ▼\n"
+ "One-hot PDFs  ──► probatablecalc  ──► empirical P(c1,c2|h)\n"
+ "                                           │\n"
+ "                                           ▼\n"
+ "                                   probatablefit  ──► smooth Pmodel(h)\n"
+ "                                                           │\n"
+ "                                                           ▼\n"
+ "                                    BMEcatPdf / MCPcatPdf / HBMEcatPdf\n"
+ "                                                           │\n"
+ "                                                           ▼\n"
+ "                                  pk[nk, nc]  ──► MAP class &amp; probability maps\n"
+ "&#96;&#96;&#96;\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 1 – Imports &amp; setup
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "import sys, os\n"
+ "import numpy as np\n"
+ "import pandas as pd\n"
+ "import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n"
+ "import matplotlib.colors as mcolors\n"
+ "import matplotlib.patches as mpatches\n"
+ "from scipy import stats\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# ── make stamps importable ─────────────────────────────────────────────────\n"
+ "REPO_ROOT = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), '..'))\n"
+ "if REPO_ROOT not in sys.path:\n"
+ "    sys.path.insert(0, REPO_ROOT)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# ── stamps categorical BME functions ───────────────────────────────────────\n"
+ "from stamps.bme.BMEcatPdf import (\n"
+ "    BMEcatPdf, MCPcatPdf, HBMEcatPdf, tune_regularization_loocv\n"
+ ")\n"
+ "from stamps.stats.dependence.probatablecalc import probatablecalc\n"
+ "from stamps.stats.dependence.probatablefit  import probatablefit\n"
+ "\n"
+ "plt.rcParams.update({'figure.dpi': 110, 'font.size': 10})\n"
+ "DATA_DIR = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), 'data')\n"
+ "print('Data directory:', DATA_DIR)\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 2 – Load data
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 1. Load and explore the Falmagne dataset\n\n"
+ "The file follows the **GeoEAS** format (title, column-count, column names, data).\n"
+ "Column 6 (&#96;soil type&#96;) records one of four soil classes: **1=silt-loam,\n"
+ "2=sandy-loam, 3=loam, 4=loamy-sand** (Dinant, Belgium classification).\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "def read_geoeas(filepath):\n"
+ "    \"\"\"Parse a GeoEAS text file. Returns (header, col_names, data_array).\"\"\"\n"
+ "    with open(filepath) as fh:\n"
+ "        lines = fh.readlines()\n"
+ "    title   = lines[0].strip()\n"
+ "    ncols   = int(lines[1].strip())\n"
+ "    col_names = [lines[2 + k].strip() for k in range(ncols)]\n"
+ "    data = np.array(\n"
+ "        [list(map(float, ln.split())) for ln in lines[2 + ncols :] if ln.strip()]\n"
+ "    )\n"
+ "    return title, col_names, data\n"
+ "\n"
+ "title, col_names, data = read_geoeas(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'Falmagne.txt'))\n"
+ "print('Title   :', title)\n"
+ "print('Columns :', col_names)\n"
+ "print('Shape   :', data.shape)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "east  = data[:, 0]          # easting  (m)\n"
+ "north = data[:, 1]          # northing (m)\n"
+ "sand  = data[:, 2]          # sand content (%)\n"
+ "silt  = data[:, 3]          # silt content (%)\n"
+ "clay  = data[:, 4]          # clay content (%)\n"
+ "code  = data[:, 5].astype(int)   # soil type 1–4\n"
+ "\n"
+ "categories = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])   # the four soil types\n"
+ "nc = len(categories)\n"
+ "n  = len(code)\n"
+ "print(f'\\n{n} observations  |  {nc} categories: {categories}')\n"
+ "print('Category counts:')\n"
+ "for c in categories:\n"
+ "    print(f'  Type {c}: {np.sum(code == c):3d} ({100*np.mean(code == c):.1f}%)')\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 3 – Spatial plot of categories
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "### 1.1 Spatial distribution of soil types\n\n"
+ "Each sampling location is coloured by its observed soil type.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "CMAP4 = ['#e41a1c', '#377eb8', '#4daf4a', '#ff7f00']   # red / blue / green / orange\n"
+ "LABELS = ['Type 1 (silt-loam)', 'Type 2 (sandy-loam)',\n"
+ "          'Type 3 (loam)',       'Type 4 (loamy-sand)']\n"
+ "\n"
+ "fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))\n"
+ "for i, (cat, col, lab) in enumerate(zip(categories, CMAP4, LABELS)):\n"
+ "    mask = code == cat\n"
+ "    ax.scatter(east[mask]/1e3, north[mask]/1e3,\n"
+ "               c=col, s=40, label=lab, edgecolors='k', linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)\n"
+ "ax.set_xlabel('Easting (km)');  ax.set_ylabel('Northing (km)')\n"
+ "ax.set_title('Falmagne – observed soil types (n=118)')\n"
+ "ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='upper right')\n"
+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 4 – One-hot encoding → soft PDFs
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 2. Encoding hard data as soft PDFs\n\n"
+ "BMEcatPdf expects **soft data** – a probability mass function (PMF) over all\n"
+ "categories at each data location.  For **hard data** (known category),\n"
+ "the PMF is a one-hot vector:\n\n"
+ "$$p_s^{(i)} = [\\mathbf{1}(c_i=1),\\; \\mathbf{1}(c_i=2),\\;\n"
+ "               \\mathbf{1}(c_i=3),\\; \\mathbf{1}(c_i=4)]$$\n\n"
+ "This is the degenerate (Dirac) distribution: certainty at the observed class.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "# coordinates array\n"
+ "cs = np.column_stack([east, north])   # (118, 2)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# One-hot encoding: ps[i, k] = 1 if code[i] == categories[k], else 0\n"
+ "ps = (code[:, None] == categories[None, :]).astype(float)  # (118, 4)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('cs shape:', cs.shape)\n"
+ "print('ps shape:', ps.shape)\n"
+ "print('First 5 rows of ps:')\n"
+ "print(ps[:5])\n"
+ "print('Corresponding codes:', code[:5])\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 5 – probatablecalc: empirical bivariate probability tables
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 3. Empirical bivariate probability tables\n\n"
+ "&#96;probatablecalc&#96; estimates the joint probability\n"
+ "$P(X_i = c_1, X_j = c_2)$ for all category pairs as a function of the\n"
+ "inter-point distance $h$.  The result encodes the **spatial dependence\n"
+ "structure** of the categorical field – the analogue of the variogram for\n"
+ "continuous variables.\n\n"
+ "### Parameters\n"
+ "- **&#96;coord_limit&#96;** – edges of distance bins (metres). The first bin captures\n"
+ "  collocated points ($h=0$); subsequent bins cover user-defined lag classes.\n"
+ "- **&#96;chunk_size&#96;** – memory-saving chunking (no effect on results).\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "# ── Distance bins ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n"
+ "# Rule of thumb: cover up to ~1/2 of the max data extent, with ~15-20 bins.\n"
+ "d_extent = np.sqrt((east.max()-east.min())**2 + (north.max()-north.min())**2)\n"
+ "print(f'Data extent: {d_extent/1e3:.1f} km')\n"
+ "\n"
+ "d_max_emp  = 25_000   # 25 km  (roughly 60 % of the full extent)\n"
+ "n_bins     = 20\n"
+ "coord_limit = np.concatenate([[0], np.linspace(500, d_max_emp, n_bins)])\n"
+ "print(f'Distance limits (km): {np.round(coord_limit/1e3, 1)}')\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# ── Compute empirical tables ────────────────────────────────────────────────\n"
+ "print('\\nComputing empirical bivariate probability tables ...')\n"
+ "D_emp, P_emp, O_emp = probatablecalc(cs, ps, coord_limit)\n"
+ "print(f'Done.  D shape={D_emp.shape},  P shape={P_emp.shape},  O shape={O_emp.shape}')\n"
+ "print(f'Pair counts per bin (first 6): {O_emp[:6].astype(int)}')\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 6 – visualise empirical tables
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "### 3.1 Visualise empirical probability tables\n\n"
+ "Each panel below shows how $P(X_i = c_1, X_j = c_2 \\mid h)$ varies with lag\n"
+ "$h$ for one category pair.  **Diagonal panels** (same category) show\n"
+ "auto-indicator correlograms (high near $h=0$, decaying to the marginal\n"
+ "frequency squared).  **Off-diagonal panels** show cross-category transition\n"
+ "probabilities.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "valid = O_emp &gt; 0   # only bins with data\n"
+ "D_v   = D_emp[valid]\n"
+ "\n"
+ "fig, axes = plt.subplots(nc, nc, figsize=(10, 9), sharex=True, sharey=False)\n"
+ "fig.suptitle('Empirical bivariate probability tables – Falmagne soil types', y=1.01)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "for r in range(nc):\n"
+ "    for c_ in range(nc):\n"
+ "        ax = axes[r, c_]\n"
+ "        vals = P_emp[r, c_, :][valid]\n"
+ "        ax.plot(D_v/1e3, vals, 'o-', ms=3, color=CMAP4[r] if r == c_ else 'steelblue')\n"
+ "        ax.axhline(vals[-1] if len(vals) else 0, ls='--', lw=0.8, color='gray')\n"
+ "        if r == 0:\n"
+ "            ax.set_title(f'→ Type {c_+1}', fontsize=8)\n"
+ "        if c_ == 0:\n"
+ "            ax.set_ylabel(f'Type {r+1} →', fontsize=8)\n"
+ "        ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "fig.text(0.5, -0.01, 'Lag distance h (km)', ha='center', fontsize=9)\n"
+ "fig.text(-0.01, 0.5, 'P(X_i=row, X_j=col | h)', va='center',\n"
+ "         rotation='vertical', fontsize=9)\n"
+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 7 – probatablefit: smooth model
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 4. Fitting a smooth probability model\n\n"
+ "&#96;probatablefit&#96; applies **kernel regression smoothing** (Gaussian kernel) to\n"
+ "the empirical tables and returns fitted values at a finer distance grid\n"
+ "&#96;dfit&#96;.  This continuous &#96;Pmodel&#96; is what BMEcatPdf uses at prediction time.\n\n"
+ "### Key parameters\n"
+ "- **&#96;kstd&#96;** – kernel standard deviation (bandwidth). Larger → smoother.\n"
+ "  A good starting value is ≈ &#96;0.5 * d_max / n_bins&#96;.\n"
+ "- **&#96;options[1]&#96;** – polynomial order inside the kernel window (0 = constant).\n"
+ "- **&#96;options[2]&#96;** – weight by pair count (&#96;1&#96; = recommended).\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "# ── Fitting grid ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n"
+ "n_fit  = 80\n"
+ "d_fit  = np.linspace(0, d_max_emp, n_fit)   # must not exceed max(D_emp)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "kstd   = 0.5 * d_max_emp / n_bins   # ≈ 625 m\n"
+ "opts   = [0, 0, 1]                  # no display / poly-0 / weighted\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'kstd = {kstd/1e3:.2f} km')\n"
+ "print('Fitting smooth probability model ...')\n"
+ "Pmodel = probatablefit(d_fit, D_emp, P_emp, O_emp.reshape(-1, 1), kstd, opts)\n"
+ "print(f'Pmodel shape: {Pmodel.shape}   (nc × nc × n_fit)')\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# dfit / Pmodel are the inputs to BMEcatPdf\n"
+ "dmodel = d_fit.copy()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 8 – plot fitted model
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "fig, axes = plt.subplots(nc, nc, figsize=(10, 9), sharex=True)\n"
+ "fig.suptitle('Fitted smooth probability model (kernel regression)', y=1.01)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "for r in range(nc):\n"
+ "    for c_ in range(nc):\n"
+ "        ax = axes[r, c_]\n"
+ "        # empirical (dots)\n"
+ "        ax.plot(D_v/1e3, P_emp[r, c_, :][valid], 'o', ms=3,\n"
+ "                color='gray', alpha=0.6, label='empirical')\n"
+ "        # fitted (line)\n"
+ "        ax.plot(d_fit/1e3, Pmodel[r, c_, :], '-',\n"
+ "                color=CMAP4[r] if r == c_ else 'steelblue',\n"
+ "                lw=1.5, label='fitted')\n"
+ "        if r == 0:\n"
+ "            ax.set_title(f'→ Type {c_+1}', fontsize=8)\n"
+ "        if c_ == 0:\n"
+ "            ax.set_ylabel(f'Type {r+1} →', fontsize=8)\n"
+ "        ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "handles = [plt.Line2D([0],[0], ls='none', marker='o', color='gray', label='Empirical'),\n"
+ "           plt.Line2D([0],[0], lw=1.5, color='steelblue', label='Fitted model')]\n"
+ "fig.legend(handles=handles, loc='lower center', ncol=2, fontsize=8)\n"
+ "fig.text(0.5, 0.01, 'Lag distance h (km)', ha='center', fontsize=9)\n"
+ "fig.text(-0.01, 0.5, 'P(X_i=row, X_j=col | h)', va='center',\n"
+ "         rotation='vertical', fontsize=9)\n"
+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 9 – build estimation grid
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 5. Build the estimation grid\n\n"
+ "We create a regular &#96;nkx × nky&#96; grid covering the data extent.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "nkx, nky = 50, 50\n"
+ "x_grid = np.linspace(east.min(),  east.max(),  nkx)\n"
+ "y_grid = np.linspace(north.min(), north.max(), nky)\n"
+ "XX, YY = np.meshgrid(x_grid, y_grid)\n"
+ "ck = np.column_stack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()])   # (nk, 2)\n"
+ "nk = ck.shape[0]\n"
+ "print(f'Estimation grid: {nkx} × {nky} = {nk} nodes')\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 10 – neighbourhood parameters
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 6. Neighbourhood parameters\n\n"
+ "| Parameter | Description |\n"
+ "|-----------|-------------|\n"
+ "| &#96;nsmax&#96;   | Max soft-data neighbours to include in the ME table |\n"
+ "| &#96;dmax&#96;    | Maximum search radius (metres) |\n\n"
+ "**Guideline:** &#96;dmax&#96; should cover the correlation range of the fitted\n"
+ "probability model (~5–15 km for this dataset), and &#96;nsmax ≤ 10&#96; keeps\n"
+ "the ME optimisation tractable.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "nsmax    = 8        # max neighbours in the ME table\n"
+ "dmax_bme = 15_000.  # 15 km search radius\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# Estimator options (shared by all three methods)\n"
+ "base_options = dict(\n"
+ "    show_progress  = 0,\n"
+ "    tol            = 1e-4,\n"
+ "    estimator      = 'MPL',    # Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood (fast &amp; stable)\n"
+ "    model_structure= 'full',   # use all (nsmax choose 2) bivariate constraints\n"
+ ")\n"
+ "print('nsmax:', nsmax, '  dmax:', dmax_bme/1e3, 'km')\n"
+ "print('Estimator options:', base_options)\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 11 – BMEcatPdf estimation
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 7. BME categorical estimation (BMEcatPdf)\n\n"
+ "**BMEcatPdf** is the rigorous Bayesian Maximum Entropy estimator.  For each\n"
+ "estimation node it:\n\n"
+ "1. Finds the &#96;nsmax&#96; nearest data points within &#96;dmax&#96;.\n"
+ "2. Builds the bivariate probability constraints from &#96;Pmodel&#96;.\n"
+ "3. Solves a Maximum Entropy optimisation to get the prior multivariate PMF\n"
+ "   $f(X_k, X_{s_1}, \\dots, X_{s_m})$.\n"
+ "4. Multiplies by the observed soft data PDFs to get the unnormalised\n"
+ "   posterior, then marginalises over the neighbours to obtain\n"
+ "   $P(X_k = c \\mid \\text{data})$.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "import time\n"
+ "\n"
+ "bme_options = {**base_options, 'show_progress': 1}\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'Running BMEcatPdf on {nk} nodes ...')\n"
+ "t0 = time.perf_counter()\n"
+ "pk_bme = BMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                   nsmax=nsmax, dmax=dmax_bme, options=bme_options)\n"
+ "t_bme = time.perf_counter() - t0\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'\\nBMEcatPdf finished in {t_bme:.1f}s  ({t_bme/nk*1000:.1f} ms/node)')\n"
+ "print('pk_bme shape:', pk_bme.shape)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# MAP estimate: category with highest posterior probability\n"
+ "map_bme = categories[np.argmax(pk_bme, axis=1)]   # (nk,)\n"
+ "# Maximum posterior probability (confidence)\n"
+ "maxp_bme = pk_bme.max(axis=1)\n"
+ "print('BME MAP class distribution:', {c: int(np.sum(map_bme == c)) for c in categories})\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 12 – MCPcatPdf (fast)
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 8. MCP fast approximation (MCPcatPdf)\n\n"
+ "**MCPcatPdf** (Maximum Conditional Probability) approximates the BME posterior\n"
+ "by assuming that the data points are **conditionally independent given\n"
+ "the estimation point**.  This avoids the ME optimisation and is therefore\n"
+ "orders of magnitude faster, at the cost of some accuracy when data are\n"
+ "spatially clustered.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "mcp_options = {**base_options, 'show_progress': 0}\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'Running MCPcatPdf on {nk} nodes ...')\n"
+ "t0 = time.perf_counter()\n"
+ "pk_mcp = MCPcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                   nsmax=nsmax, dmax=dmax_bme, options=mcp_options)\n"
+ "t_mcp = time.perf_counter() - t0\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'MCPcatPdf finished in {t_mcp:.1f}s  ({t_mcp/nk*1000:.1f} ms/node)')\n"
+ "map_mcp  = categories[np.argmax(pk_mcp, axis=1)]\n"
+ "maxp_mcp = pk_mcp.max(axis=1)\n"
+ "print('MCP speed-up vs BME: ×{:.0f}'.format(t_bme / t_mcp if t_mcp &gt; 0 else np.inf))\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 13 – HBMEcatPdf
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 9. Hybrid BME (HBMEcatPdf)\n\n"
+ "**HBMEcatPdf** provides a middle ground:\n\n"
+ "1. **Step 1 (regional prior):** Run MCP with many neighbours (&#96;nsmax_total&#96;)\n"
+ "   to summarise the regional trend as a soft prior.\n"
+ "2. **Step 2 (local update):** Run BME with only the &#96;nsmax&#96; closest neighbours,\n"
+ "   using the MCP prior.  This keeps the ME table small while benefiting from a\n"
+ "   spatially varying prior.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "hbme_options = {**base_options,\n"
+ "                'nsmax_total': 40,    # neighbours for the MCP prior step\n"
+ "                'show_progress': 0}\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'Running HBMEcatPdf on {nk} nodes ...')\n"
+ "t0 = time.perf_counter()\n"
+ "pk_hbme = HBMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                     nsmax=nsmax, dmax=dmax_bme, options=hbme_options)\n"
+ "t_hbme = time.perf_counter() - t0\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print(f'HBMEcatPdf finished in {t_hbme:.1f}s  ({t_hbme/nk*1000:.1f} ms/node)')\n"
+ "map_hbme  = categories[np.argmax(pk_hbme, axis=1)]\n"
+ "maxp_hbme = pk_hbme.max(axis=1)\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "# Build a ListedColormap for the 4 soil types\n"

+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 11. Posterior uncertainty maps\n\n"

+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "def plot_map_prob(ax, prob_grid, title):\n"

+

+ "        f'type{cat}', ['white', col]\n"
+ "    )\n"
+ "    im = ax.pcolormesh(XX/1e3, YY/1e3, prob_cat,\n"
+ "                       cmap=cmap_i, vmin=0, vmax=1, shading='auto')\n"
+ "    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label=f'P(Type {cat})')\n"
+ "    # overlay data\n"
+ "    for c2 in categories:\n"
+ "        m = code == c2\n"

+ "                   linewidths=0.4, zorder=4)\n"
+ "    ax.set_title(f'BME P(soil = {cat}: {LABELS[idx]})', fontsize=9)\n"

+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 17 – LOOCV validation
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 13. Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV)\n\n"
+ "We evaluate predictive accuracy by predicting each data point using all\n"
+ "remaining points, then comparing the predicted MAP class with the true class.\n\n"
+ "**Metrics used:**\n"
+ "- **Accuracy** – fraction of correctly predicted MAP classes.\n"
+ "- **Mean log-likelihood** – $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\log P(\\hat{X}_i = c_i)$;\n"
+ "  higher is better; measures probabilistic calibration.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "def loocv_accuracy(cs_data, ps_data, code_data, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                   nsmax, dmax, options, categories, method_fn):\n"
+ "    \"\"\"Leave-One-Out cross-validation for a categorical estimator.\"\"\"\n"
+ "    n = cs_data.shape[0]\n"
+ "    correct = 0\n"
+ "    log_liks = []\n"
+ "\n"
+ "    opts = {**options, 'show_progress': 0}\n"
+ "\n"
+ "    for i in range(n):\n"
+ "        ck_i   = cs_data[i:i+1, :]          # hold-out location\n"
+ "        cs_loo = np.delete(cs_data, i, 0)   # training coordinates\n"
+ "        ps_loo = np.delete(ps_data, i, 0)   # training PDFs\n"
+ "\n"
+ "        pk_i = method_fn(ck_i, cs_loo, ps_loo,\n"
+ "                         dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options=opts)\n"
+ "        pred_cat = categories[np.argmax(pk_i[0])]\n"
+ "        true_cat = code_data[i]\n"
+ "        correct += (pred_cat == true_cat)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "        # log-likelihood of the true category\n"
+ "        true_idx = np.where(categories == true_cat)[0][0]\n"
+ "        prob_true = np.clip(pk_i[0, true_idx], 1e-15, 1.0)\n"
+ "        log_liks.append(np.log(prob_true))\n"
+ "\n"
+ "    accuracy   = correct / n\n"
+ "    mean_ll    = np.mean(log_liks)\n"
+ "    return accuracy, mean_ll\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('Running LOOCV for BMEcatPdf  ...')\n"
+ "acc_bme,  ll_bme  = loocv_accuracy(cs, ps, code, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                                    nsmax, dmax_bme, base_options,\n"
+ "                                    categories, BMEcatPdf)\n"
+ "print(f'  BME  – Accuracy: {acc_bme:.3f}  |  Mean log-likelihood: {ll_bme:.3f}')\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('Running LOOCV for MCPcatPdf  ...')\n"
+ "acc_mcp,  ll_mcp  = loocv_accuracy(cs, ps, code, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                                    nsmax, dmax_bme, base_options,\n"
+ "                                    categories, MCPcatPdf)\n"
+ "print(f'  MCP  – Accuracy: {acc_mcp:.3f}  |  Mean log-likelihood: {ll_mcp:.3f}')\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('Running LOOCV for HBMEcatPdf ...')\n"
+ "hbme_loocv_opts = {**base_options, 'nsmax_total': 40}\n"
+ "acc_hbme, ll_hbme = loocv_accuracy(cs, ps, code, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                                    nsmax, dmax_bme, hbme_loocv_opts,\n"
+ "                                    categories, HBMEcatPdf)\n"
+ "print(f'  HBME – Accuracy: {acc_hbme:.3f}  |  Mean log-likelihood: {ll_hbme:.3f}')\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 18 – LOOCV bar chart
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "methods   = ['BMEcatPdf', 'MCPcatPdf', 'HBMEcatPdf']\n"
+ "accuracies = [acc_bme,  acc_mcp,  acc_hbme]\n"
+ "log_liks_  = [ll_bme,   ll_mcp,   ll_hbme]\n"
+ "\n"
+ "fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))\n"
+ "\n"
+ "bar_colors = ['#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c']\n"
+ "axes[0].bar(methods, accuracies, color=bar_colors, edgecolor='k')\n"
+ "axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1);  axes[0].set_ylabel('LOOCV Accuracy')\n"
+ "axes[0].set_title('Classification Accuracy (LOOCV)')\n"
+ "for i, v in enumerate(accuracies):\n"
+ "    axes[0].text(i, v + 0.01, f'{v:.3f}', ha='center', fontsize=10)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "axes[1].bar(methods, log_liks_, color=bar_colors, edgecolor='k')\n"
+ "axes[1].set_ylabel('Mean Log-Likelihood')\n"
+ "axes[1].set_title('Probabilistic Score – Mean Log-Likelihood (LOOCV)')\n"
+ "for i, v in enumerate(log_liks_):\n"
+ "    axes[1].text(i, v + 0.002, f'{v:.3f}', ha='center', fontsize=10)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('\\nSummary table:')\n"
+ "df_res = pd.DataFrame({'Method': methods,\n"
+ "                        'LOOCV Accuracy': accuracies,\n"
+ "                        'Mean Log-Lik' : log_liks_})\n"
+ "print(df_res.to_string(index=False))\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 19 – Estimator comparison side-by-side per category
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 14. Per-category precision recall\n\n"
+ "We compute a simple **per-class precision and recall** from the LOOCV\n"
+ "predictions (MAP class vs. true class) to see which soil types are most\n"
+ "or least well predicted.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "def loocv_predictions(cs_data, ps_data, code_data, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                       nsmax, dmax, options, categories, method_fn):\n"
+ "    \"\"\"Return array of predicted MAP classes for LOOCV.\"\"\"\n"
+ "    n    = cs_data.shape[0]\n"
+ "    preds = np.zeros(n, dtype=int)\n"
+ "    opts  = {**options, 'show_progress': 0}\n"
+ "    for i in range(n):\n"
+ "        ck_i   = cs_data[i:i+1, :]\n"
+ "        cs_loo = np.delete(cs_data, i, 0)\n"
+ "        ps_loo = np.delete(ps_data, i, 0)\n"
+ "        pk_i   = method_fn(ck_i, cs_loo, ps_loo,\n"
+ "                           dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options=opts)\n"
+ "        preds[i] = categories[np.argmax(pk_i[0])]\n"
+ "    return preds\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('Computing per-class metrics for BMEcatPdf ...')\n"
+ "preds_bme = loocv_predictions(cs, ps, code, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                               nsmax, dmax_bme, base_options, categories, BMEcatPdf)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# Confusion matrix\n"
+ "conf = np.zeros((nc, nc), dtype=int)\n"
+ "for true_c, pred_c in zip(code, preds_bme):\n"
+ "    r_idx = np.where(categories == true_c)[0][0]\n"
+ "    c_idx = np.where(categories == pred_c)[0][0]\n"
+ "    conf[r_idx, c_idx] += 1\n"
+ "\n"
+ "print('\\nConfusion matrix (rows=true, cols=predicted):')\n"
+ "df_conf = pd.DataFrame(conf,\n"
+ "    index   = [f'True {c}' for c in categories],\n"
+ "    columns = [f'Pred {c}' for c in categories])\n"
+ "print(df_conf)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# Per-class precision and recall\n"
+ "precision = np.diag(conf) / conf.sum(axis=0).clip(min=1)\n"
+ "recall    = np.diag(conf) / conf.sum(axis=1).clip(min=1)\n"
+ "f1_score  = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall).clip(min=1e-9)\n"
+ "\n"
+ "df_pr = pd.DataFrame({'Category': [f'Type {c}' for c in categories],\n"
+ "                       'Precision': precision,\n"
+ "                       'Recall'   : recall,\n"
+ "                       'F1-score' : f1_score})\n"
+ "print('\\nPer-class precision / recall (BMEcatPdf LOOCV):')\n"
+ "print(df_pr.to_string(index=False))\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 20 – Confusion matrix heatmap
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# Confusion matrix\n"
+ "im = axes[0].imshow(conf, cmap='Blues', vmin=0)\n"
+ "for r in range(nc):\n"
+ "    for c_ in range(nc):\n"
+ "        axes[0].text(c_, r, str(conf[r, c_]),\n"
+ "                     ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12)\n"
+ "axes[0].set_xticks(range(nc));  axes[0].set_xticklabels([f'Pred {c}' for c in categories])\n"
+ "axes[0].set_yticks(range(nc));  axes[0].set_yticklabels([f'True {c}' for c in categories])\n"
+ "axes[0].set_title('Confusion Matrix – BMEcatPdf (LOOCV)', fontsize=10)\n"
+ "plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0])\n"
+ "\n"
+ "# Bar chart: precision / recall\n"
+ "x = np.arange(nc)\n"
+ "w = 0.3\n"
+ "axes[1].bar(x - w/2, precision, width=w, label='Precision', color='steelblue')\n"
+ "axes[1].bar(x + w/2, recall,    width=w, label='Recall',    color='darkorange')\n"
+ "axes[1].set_xticks(x)\n"
+ "axes[1].set_xticklabels([f'Type {c}' for c in categories])\n"
+ "axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1.05);  axes[1].set_ylabel('Score')\n"
+ "axes[1].set_title('Per-Class Precision &amp; Recall – BMEcatPdf (LOOCV)', fontsize=10)\n"
+ "axes[1].legend()\n"
+ "\n"
+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 21 – Spatial error map (LOOCV)
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "### 14.1 Spatial distribution of LOOCV errors\n\n"

+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "correct_mask   = preds_bme == code\n"
+ "incorrect_mask = ~correct_mask\n"
+ "\n"
+ "fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))\n"
+ "for cat, col in zip(categories, CMAP4):\n"

+ "    # Misclassified (marked with 'x')\n"

+ "\n"
+ "ax.set_xlabel('Easting (km)');  ax.set_ylabel('Northing (km)')\n"
+ "ax.set_title(f'LOOCV errors – BMEcatPdf  '\n"
+ "             f'(correct: {correct_mask.sum()}/{n}, '\n"
+ "             f'wrong: {incorrect_mask.sum()}/{n})')\n"
+ "ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2)\n"
+ "plt.tight_layout();  plt.show()\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ # Cell 22 – Sensitivity to nsmax
+ # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(
+ "## 15. Sensitivity analysis – effect of &#96;nsmax&#96;\n\n"
+ "We use the fast **MCPcatPdf** estimator to quickly assess how the number of\n"
+ "neighbours influences LOOCV accuracy.\n"
+ ))
+ 
+ cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(
+ "nsmax_grid  = [2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16]\n"
+ "acc_vs_ns   = []\n"
+ "ll_vs_ns    = []\n"
+ "\n"
+ "for ns in nsmax_grid:\n"
+ "    a, ll = loocv_accuracy(cs, ps, code, dmodel, Pmodel,\n"
+ "                           ns, dmax_bme, base_options,\n"
+ "                           categories, MCPcatPdf)\n"
+ "    acc_vs_ns.append(a)\n"
+ "    ll_vs_ns.append(ll)\n"
+ "    print(f'  nsmax={ns:3d}  accuracy={a:.3f}  log-lik={ll:.3f}')\n"
```

Clean. Here's what was wrong and what was fixed:

---

### Root cause

`probatablefit` builds a symmetric distance vector with `np.vstack`:

```python
dsym = np.vstack((np.flipud(-d), d[1:nd]))
osym = np.vstack((np.flipud(o),  o[1:nd]))
```

`np.vstack` on **1-D arrays** first promotes each to a `(1, n)` row-vector, so:
- `np.flipud(-d)` → `(1, 21)` (full array)  
- `d[1:nd]` → `(1, 20)` (all but first element)  

Sizes differ along axis 1 → **`ValueError`**.

The function was written expecting **column vectors** `(n, 1)`, but `probatablecalc` returns plain 1-D arrays.

### Fix applied (`probatablefit.py`)

Added two lines right after the range-check to normalise both inputs to column vectors before any `vstack` is called:

```python
d = np.asarray(d, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
o = np.asarray(o, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
```

This makes the function accept **both** 1-D arrays (as returned by `probatablecalc`) and pre-shaped column vectors without any change to the calling notebook.

Now I have the complete picture. Let me explain the root cause precisely and then fix both the code and the notebook.

**Root Cause — Mathematical Proof:**

The MCP log-posterior is:
```
log p(X₀=c) ∝ (1−n)·log P_prior(c) + Σₖ log[ Σ_{c'} P_biv(Xₖ=c', X₀=c)·pₖ(c') ]
```

Beyond the correlation range (~8–10 km), the bivariate table factorizes to independence:
```
P_biv(Xₖ=c', X₀=c) ≈ P(c') · P(c)
```
so the k-th term collapses to `log P(c) + const_k`.  With 40 neighbours (`nsmax_total=40`) mostly beyond the ~10 km correlation range, the whole sum becomes `n·log P(c)`, which, combined with the `(1−n)·log P_prior` uniform term, gives exactly `log P(c)` — **the global marginal probability, identical at every estimation point**.  
That constant "prior" is then passed into every BME call, so BME adds only small local corrections that are washed out, making the HBME map nearly flat.

**Fix:**
1. Add a `dmax_mcp` option to `HBMEcatPdf` so the MCP prior step can be restricted to the correlation range.
2. Fix the notebook to use `dmax_mcp = 8_000` (≈ correlation range) and `nsmax_total = 15`.
3. Document the degeneration behaviour in the docstring.

All three changes are done. Here is the complete explanation:

---

## Root Cause — Mathematical Proof

The MCP log-posterior is:
$$\log p(X_0{=}c) \propto (1-n)\log P_\text{prior}(c) + \sum_k \log\!\left[\sum_{c'} P_\text{biv}(X_k{=}c',\, X_0{=}c)\cdot p_k(c')\right]$$

For neighbours **beyond the covariance correlation range** (~8–10 km), the bivariate table factorises:
$$P_\text{biv}(X_k{=}c',\, X_0{=}c) \approx P(c')\cdot P(c)$$

Each such out-of-range neighbour contributes exactly `log P(c)` to the sum. With `nsmax_total=40` neighbours (where most are decorrelated across the 21×24 km Falmagne area), the sum gives:

$$\log p(X_0{=}c) \approx (1-40)\log P(c) + 40\log P(c) = \log P(c) + \text{const}$$

**The MCP prior degenerates to the global marginal frequency — identical at every estimation location.** The subsequent BME local-update step then starts from the same flat prior everywhere, producing nearly constant HBME output.

## Three Fixes Applied

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `BMEcatPdf.py` – `HBMEcatPdf` | Added `dmax_mcp` option (defaults to `dmax`). The MCP prior step now uses this separate, smaller radius. Default `nsmax_total` changed from `100` → `20`. Docstring has the full mathematical warning. |
| `make_nb09.py` – HBME cell | `nsmax_total: 40` → `nsmax_total = 15`, new `dmax_mcp = 8_000` (≈ correlation range). Added a clear markdown section with the $\log P(c)$ proof and the *rule of thumb*: **set `dmax_mcp` ≈ correlation range**. |
| `make_nb09.py` – LOOCV cell | Updated HBME options to use the same `nsmax_total` / `dmax_mcp` variables. |

**Rule of thumb:** set `dmax_mcp` ≈ covariance correlation range and `nsmax_total` ≈ 2–3× `nsmax`. This ensures MCP only aggregates spatially correlated evidence, giving a prior that varies meaningfully across space before the BME local refinement step.

The user is asking for a detailed mathematical derivation of why including more independent (decorrelated) data makes the MCP prior shrink to the global marginal. They also want to understand why HBME results are even closer to global marginals than MCP alone, and why HBME and MCP have higher estimation uncertainty compared to BME despite using more data.

Let me provide a thorough mathematical explanation.

**Part 1: Why MCP degenerates to global marginal with decorrelated data**

The MCP formula (from equation 37 in the image) is:

$$p(x_0 | x_1=\chi_1, ..., x_m=\chi_m, x_{m+1}=p_s(x_{m+1}), ...) = \frac{p(x_0)^{1-(m+n)} \prod_{k=1}^m p(x_k=\chi_k, x_0) \prod_{k=m+1}^{m+n} \sum_{x_k} p(x_k,

x_0) p_s(x_k)}{\sum_{x_0} [\text{same numerator}]}$$

When I take the log form for categorical variables with hard observations, the posterior probability becomes proportional to a weighted combination of the prior and the joint probabilities with neighbors. At distances beyond the correlation range, those bivariate probabilities factor into independent marginals, so each neighbor contributes a term that's essentially just the marginal probability of that neighbor's value times the prior on the target variable.

Summing across all neighbors, the prior term gets multiplied by the number of neighbors, which exactly cancels with the coefficient in front of it, leaving only a constant offset. This means the posterior simplifies to just the global marginal probability—the spatial information washes out entirely.

Now looking at why HBME pushes even further toward the global marginals compared to MCP alone... The posterior combines the prior with a likelihood term derived from the ME joint and all the marginals, but when the prior itself approximates the global marginal P(c), it ends up double-counting that information—both through the explicit prior and through the ME joint structure. This dual encoding means the posterior gets pulled even more strongly toward the global marginal, potentially overwhelming the local data signal.

Let me reconsider the comparison more carefully: standard BME with a uniform prior gives a posterior proportional to the likelihood alone, while HBME with an MCP prior proportional to P(c) multiplies that same likelihood by an extra P(c) factor. This is a great question that touches on fundamental information theory and the structure of MCP. Let me give you a rigorous step-by-step derivation for all three parts.

---

## Part 1 — Why Decorrelated Neighbours Collapse MCP to the Global Marginal

### Setup

From Equation (37) in your image, the MCP posterior for categorical \(X_0\) given \(n\) soft/hard neighbours is:

$$\log p(x_0 = c) \;\propto\; \underbrace{(1 - n)\log p(c)}_{\text{prior term}} \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} \log \!\left[\sum_{c'} p(x_k = c',\, x_0 = c)\; p_k(c')\right]$$

### Step 1 — Bivariate Table Factorises at Large Distance

The bivariate model \(p(x_k = c',\, x_0 = c)\) is built from the probability table \(P_\text{model}(h)\). At lag \(h\) **beyond the correlation range** \(a\), the two random variables become statistically independent:

$$p(x_k = c',\, x_0 = c) \;\xrightarrow{h \gg a}\; p(c')\cdot p(c)$$

### Step 2 — Substitute into Each Log Term

For each neighbour \(k\) beyond the range, with hard data \(p_k(c') = \mathbf{1}[c' = \chi_k]\):

$$\sum_{c'} p(x_k = c',\, x_0 = c)\; p_k(c') = \sum_{c'} p(c') p(c) \cdot \mathbf{1}[c' = \chi_k] = p(\chi_k)\cdot p(c)$$

Taking the log:

$$\log\!\left[\sum_{c'} p(x_k{=}c', x_0{=}c)\;p_k(c')\right] = \underbrace{\log p(\chi_k)}_{\text{constant w.r.t.} c} + \log p(c)$$

### Step 3 — Sum Over All \(n\) Decorrelated Neighbours

$$\log p(x_0 = c) \;\propto\; (1-n)\log p(c) \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{n}\left[\log p(\chi_k) + \log p(c)\right]$$

$$= (1-n)\log p(c) + n\log p(c) + \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log p(\chi_k)}_{\text{constant w.r.t.}\; c}$$

$$\boxed{= \log p(c) + \text{const}}$$

### Step 4 — Normalise

$$p(x_0 = c \mid \text{all decorrelated data}) = \frac{p(c)}{\sum_{c'} p(c')} = p(c)$$

**Conclusion:** No matter how many decorrelated neighbours you add, the MCP posterior is exactly the global marginal \(p(c)\) — identical at every estimation point. The \(n\) pairs of terms \((1-n)\) and \(+n\) *cancel exactly*, so more decorrelated data contributes zero new spatial information.

---

## Part 2 — Why HBME Is Even Flatter Than MCP

HBME feeds the MCP prior \(\hat{p}_\text{MCP}(c) \approx p(c)\) into `producttablepdf` as the dimension-0 marginal, which multiplies the ME joint prior:

$$P_\text{post}(X_0 = c,\, X_1,\ldots,X_m) \;\propto\; P_\text{ME}(c, X_1,\ldots) \cdot \hat{p}_\text{MCP}(c) \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{m} p_k(X_k)$$

### The Double-Counting Problem

The ME prior \(P_\text{ME}\) is built from the bivariate probability model. Its **marginal at dimension 0** satisfies, for any neighbour \(k\):

$$\sum_{X_1,\ldots,X_m} P_\text{ME}(c, X_1,\ldots,X_m) = p_\text{ME,marginal}(c) \approx p(c)$$

because the bivariate table itself sums to the global marginal. So the BME posterior **already encodes \(p(c)\)** through the ME joint prior.

When the MCP prior \(\hat{p}_\text{MCP}(c) \approx p(c)\) is also multiplied at dim 0, the global marginal is **counted twice**:

$$p_\text{HBME}(c) \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(c)}_{\text{from ME prior}} \cdot \underbrace{p(c)}_{\text{from MCP prior}} \cdot L(c)$$

$$= p(c)^2 \cdot L(c)$$

### Effect on the Posterior

Suppose \(p(c) = [0.40,\ 0.30,\ 0.20,\ 0.10]\) and \(L(c)\) is locally informative \(= [0.5,\ 0.3,\ 0.1,\ 0.1]\) (normalised). Then:

| Method | Formula | Raw | Normalised MAP cat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BME** | \(1/4 \cdot L(c)\) | \([0.50, 0.30, 0.10, 0.10]\) | Cat 1, 50% |
| **MCP prior** | \(p(c)\) | \([0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10]\) | Cat 1, 40% |
| **HBME** | \(p(c)^2 \cdot L(c)\) | \([0.08, 0.027, 0.002, 0.001]\) → norm | Cat 1, 72% |

So HBME doesn't flatten the MAP class — it actually *amplifies* the dominant category. However, because the \(p(c)\) is the **same at every location** (from the decorrelated MCP prior), the map lacks spatial variation. Near a local cluster of Category 2 where BME would predict Cat 2, HBME still over-weights Cat 1 through the global \(p(c)^2\) factor. The result is a map that is spatially monotone toward the globally dominant category.

The fundamental issue: **the MCP prior and the ME prior share the same marginal \(p(c)\) source**. Treating them as independent and multiplying them double-counts the global-marginal information.

---

## Part 3 — Why MCP/HBME Have Higher Uncertainty Than BME Despite More Data

This is an information-theoretic phenomenon: **more data is not always more informative**.

### Formal Argument via Information Content

The information that neighbour \(k\) at distance \(h_k\) provides about \(X_0\) is quantified by the mutual information:

$$I(X_0;\, X_k) = \sum_{c,c'} p(c,c') \log \frac{p(c,c')}{p(c)p(c')}$$

At large distances (\(h_k \gg a\)): \(p(c,c') \to p(c)p(c')\), so:

$$I(X_0;\, X_k) \;\to\; 0 \quad \text{as}\; h_k \to \infty$$

BME with \(n_\text{BME} = 8\) **close** neighbours may have total information:

$$I_\text{BME} = \sum_{k=1}^{8} I(X_0;\, X_k \mid h_k \leq a) \gg 0$$

MCP with \(n_\text{MCP} = 40\) neighbours, mostly beyond range:

$$I_\text{MCP} = \underbrace{\sum_{k: h_k \leq a} I(X_0;\, X_k)}_{\text{small count, high per-point}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k: h_k > a} 0}_{\approx 0} \;\approx\; I_\text{BME,close\;subset}$$

The 32 extra decorrelated neighbours add **zero information** but do consume the "weight budget" in the MCP formula (the \((1-n)\) prior-dilution factor), leaving less room for the informative close neighbours.

### Why the Posterior Is Flatter (Higher Uncertainty)

For BME near a hard data point of category \(\chi_k\):
$$p_\text{BME}(c) \sim \text{concentrated near}\; \chi_k, \quad \max_c p_\text{BME}(c) \approx 0.8\text{–}1.0$$

For MCP with many decorrelated votes that cancel:
$$p_\text{MCP}(c) \approx p(c), \quad \max_c p_\text{MCP}(c) \approx 0.35\text{–}0.45$$

The uncertainty (entropy) satisfies:
$$H[p_\text{MCP}] = -\sum_c p(c)\log p(c) \;>\; H[p_\text{BME}]$$

### Intuitive Analogy

Imagine polling 8 people who live in your neighbourhood vs. 40 people drawn from the entire city about what your local area is like. The 8 locals give sharp, consistent evidence. The 40 city-wide respondents (most of whom have never visited) give answers that average to the city-wide distribution, producing maximum *uncertainty* about your specific neighbourhood. Adding more uncorrelated respondents does not reduce uncertainty — it regresses to the mean.

---

## Summary Table

| Effect | Cause | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| MCP → global marginal | Beyond-range neighbours factorize: \(p(c', c) \to p(c') p(c)\); the \((1-n)\) and \(+n\log p(c)\) terms cancel | MCP map is spatially flat |
| HBME even flatter | MCP prior \(\approx p(c)\) multiplied against ME prior (whose marginal is already \(p(c)\)) → double-counted \(p(c)^2\) | HBME biased toward globally dominant category |
| More data → more uncertainty | Decorrelated data has zero mutual information with \(X_0\); it dilutes the informative close-range signal | MCP/HBME posteriors are flatter (higher entropy) than BME with fewer, closer neighbours |

**Practical fix (already implemented):** Set `dmax_mcp` ≈ correlation range \(a\) so that MCP uses *only* correlated neighbours, preserving nonzero \(I(X_0; X_k)\) for every included data point. This ensures \(\hat{p}_\text{MCP}(c)\) is spatially varying and genuinely informative when passed as the BME prior.

## What the ME Prior `Pkh_` Is — Traced Through the Code

### Step 1 — `maxentropytable` builds the ME joint prior

In `BMEcatPdf`, line 1464:

```python
Pkh_, niter = maxentropytable(
    np.vstack((ck0, cslocal)),   # (1 + m, d)  — estimation point + m neighbours
    dmodel, Pmodel, options=options
)
```

`maxentropytable` receives coordinates for **all** `ndim = 1 + m` locations. It:

1. Computes pairwise distances between every pair of those locations (including the estimation point `ck0 = c[0]` paired with each data neighbour `c[k]`, and data neighbours paired with each other)
2. Looks up the fitted bivariate probability table `P_biv(c', c)` at each pairwise distance by interpolation from `Pmodel`
3. Solves the Maximum Entropy optimisation problem:

$$P_\text{ME}(X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_m) = \arg\max_P H[P]$$
$$\text{subject to:}\quad \sum_{X_0,\ldots \text{except } i,j} P(\ldots) = P_\text{biv}^{(i,j)}(c_i, c_j) \quad \forall \text{ pairs } (i,j),\; \forall c_i, c_j$$

The returned `Pkh_` is an `(nc, nc, …, nc)` array with `ndim` axes — the full joint prior over all locations simultaneously.

### Key property: the marginal of `Pkh_` at dimension 0

Because every bivariate table in `Pmodel` sums to the global category frequency over either argument:
$$\sum_{c'} P_\text{biv}(c, c') = p(c) \quad \text{(empirical marginal)}$$

the ME distribution's marginal at **any** single dimension, including dim 0 (the estimation point), equals the global marginal:
$$\sum_{X_1,\ldots,X_m} P_\text{ME}(c, X_1,\ldots,X_m) = p(c)$$

**This is the "ME prior" I referred to** — it is not a separate object; it is the full joint distribution `Pkh_`, and its implied marginal at the estimation location is already `p(c)` before any data is applied.

---

## Step 2 — `producttablepdf` applies the prior and data

```python
Pkh = producttablepdf(Pkh_, np.vstack((prior_to_use, pslocal)))
```

The `pdf` matrix stacked here is:

| Row | Content | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `prior_to_use` | The 1-D prior distribution at X₀ |
| 1 | `pslocal[0,:]` | Observed PDF at neighbour 1 |
| … | … | … |
| m | `pslocal[m-1,:]` | Observed PDF at neighbour m |

`producttablepdf` multiplies the ME joint by each row's vector *along its own axis*:

```python
for i in range(ndim):
    Pprod *= pdf[i, :].reshape(expand_shape)   # broadcasts over all other dims
```

The result entry is:

$$P_\text{post}(c, c_1, \ldots, c_m) = P_\text{ME}(c, c_1, \ldots, c_m) \cdot q_0(c) \cdot \prod_{k=1}^m p_k(c_k)$$

Marginalising over `dims 1…m` gives the unnormalised posterior at X₀:

$$p_\text{post}(c) \propto q_0(c) \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{c_1,\ldots,c_m} P_\text{ME}(c, c_1,\ldots,c_m) \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{m} p_k(c_k)}_{\text{ME-weighted likelihood} \;=\; L_\text{ME}(c)}$$

---

## Step 3 — The default (uniform) prior in `BMEcatPdf`

```python
uniform_prior = np.ones(ncat) / ncat   # line 1390
```

When `prior_to_use = [1/nc, 1/nc, …]`, the dim-0 multiplication in `producttablepdf` is a constant scaling — it does **not** change the relative probabilities across categories. The posterior reduces to:

$$p_\text{BME}(c) \propto L_\text{ME}(c) = \sum_{c_1,\ldots,c_m} P_\text{ME}(c, c_1,\ldots,c_m) \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{m} p_k(c_k)$$

For hard data (one-hot `pslocal`), this is simply:

$$p_\text{BME}(c) \propto P_\text{ME}(c,\, \chi_1, \chi_2, \ldots, \chi_m)$$

the joint probability under the ME distribution that X₀=c **and** all neighbours take their observed values. This varies spatially because it depends on the distances to the observed data points.

> **Conclusion:** BMEcatPdf with a uniform prior is equivalent to using the ME joint prior alone. The "prior at the estimation point" in the ME sense is already implicitly `p(c)` (global marginal), but the *effective* prior in the computation is cancelled by the uniform factor.

---

## Step 4 — How HBME replaces the uniform prior

In `HBMEcatPdf`:

```python
pk_mcp_prior = MCPcatPdf(ck0, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax_total, dmax_mcp, ...)
```

---

## Part 1 — The Double-Counting Problem with an Informative Prior

### What `L_ME(c)` really is

After marginalizing `producttablepdf`'s output over dims 1…m, the unnormalized posterior is:

$$p_\text{post}(c) \propto \underbrace{q_0(c)}_{\texttt{prior\_to\_use}} \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{c_1,\ldots,c_m} P_\text{ME}(c, c_1,\ldots,c_m) \cdot \prod_{k=1}^m p_k(c_k)}_{L_\text{ME}(c)}$$

What is `L_ME(c)` for no data (m=0)?

$$L_\text{ME}(c)\big|_{m=0} = P_\text{ME}(c) = p(c) \quad \text{(the global marginal)}$$

For hard data at m neighbours at distance → 0:

$$L_\text{ME}(c)\big|_{d\to 0} \approx \mathbf{1}[c = \chi_1] \quad \text{(one-hot)}$$

For data at large distance (beyond correlation range):

$$L_\text{ME}(c)\big|_{d\gg a} \approx p(c) \cdot P(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_m) \propto p(c)$$

So `L_ME(c)` encodes a continuum: it IS `p(c)` at large distances and departs from it only as correlated data is included. **The global marginal `p(c)` is already the "implicit prior" embedded in `L_ME(c)` when data is absent or far away.**

### The Bayes-factor correction for an XGBoost prior

Applying Bayes' theorem correctly, the likelihood of the spatial observations given `X_0 = c` is:

$$\mathcal{L}(c) = \frac{P_\text{ME}(c, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_m)}{p(c)} = \frac{L_\text{ME}(c)}{p(c)}$$

(dividing out the implicit global-marginal prior that is already inside `L_ME`). The correct posterior with an informative XGBoost prior `q(c)` is:

$$p_\text{post}(c) \propto q(c) \cdot \mathcal{L}(c) = q(c) \cdot \frac{L_\text{ME}(c)}{p(c)} = \frac{q(c)}{p(c)} \cdot L_\text{ME}(c)$$

**Therefore, the correct value to pass as `prior_pdf_at_ck` is the Bayes factor:**

$$\texttt{prior\_to\_use}(c) = \frac{q_\text{XGB}(c)}{p(c)}$$

**not** the raw XGBoost probability `q(c)`. You can verify the two limits:

| Distance regime | `L_ME(c)` | Posterior `∝ q(c)/p(c) · L_ME` | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| No data | `p(c)` | `q(c)/p(c) · p(c)` | `= q(c)` ✓ recovers XGB prior |
| Close hard data | `≈ 1[c=χ]` | `q(c)/p(c) · 1[c=χ]` | `∝ q(χ)` ✓ data dominates, scaled by prior |

If you instead pass `prior_to_use = q(c)` directly (without dividing by `p(c)`), the posterior far from data is `∝ q(c)·p(c)` — a mixture of XGBoost and global marginal, which double-counts spatial frequency information.

### Practical implementation of `BMEpriorPDF`

In Python, the corrected prior to supply to `BMEcatPdf` would be:

```python
# global_marginal: array (nc,) of empirical category frequencies
# xgb_prior_at_ck: array (nk, nc) from XGBoost predictions

# Bayes-factor correction: divide out the global marginal
bayes_factor = xgb_prior_at_ck / global_marginal[np.newaxis, :]

# Normalize each row (Bayes factors need not sum to 1)
bayes_factor /= bayes_factor.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

bme_options = {
    ...
    'prior_pdf_at_ck': bayes_factor   # shape (nk, nc)
}
pk = BMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options=bme_options)
```

This is well-posed: the XGBoost prior is derived from non-spatial covariates (geology, elevation, texture), which are genuinely independent of the spatial category observations that drive `L_ME`. There is no circular dependency.

---

## Part 2 — Is the HBME Limited-Buffer Approach Mathematically Sound?

### Where data-leakage occurs

Consider the data points within `dmax_mcp = 8 km` around an estimation point `ck0`. Call this set **S_mcp**. The data points within `dmax_bme = 15 km` form a larger set **S_bme**, where **S_mcp ⊂ S_bme**.

The HBME steps are:

| Step | Function | Data used |
|---|---|---|
| 1. MCP prior | `MCPcatPdf(…, dmax=dmax_mcp)` | **S_mcp** |
| 2. BME update | `BMEcatPdf(…, prior=pk_mcp, dmax=dmax_bme)` | **S_bme** (**includes S_mcp**) |

The data in **S_mcp** appears in **both** steps. In a strict Bayesian sense, the prior must be independent of the likelihood data. Here it is not: the MCP prior is a posterior computed from **S_mcp**, and the BME step then uses the same **S_mcp** data again as part of its likelihood via `L_ME(c)`.

### What this means mathematically

The "true" Bayesian posterior (if we had a correct joint prior over all categories simultaneously) would be:

$$p_\text{true}(c \mid \text{all data}) \propto p_\text{external\_prior}(c) \cdot P_\text{ME}(c, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_m)$$

The HBME approximation computes instead:

$$p_\text{HBME}(c) \propto \underbrace{p_\text{MCP}(c \mid \text{S\_mcp})}_{\text{posterior from S\_mcp, not a prior}} \cdot P_\text{ME}(c, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_m \in \text{S\_bme})$$

This means data in **S_mcp** enters the formula twice:
- Once inside `p_MCP(c | S_mcp)` (through MCP's bivariate likelihood terms)
- Once inside `P_ME(c, S_bme)` (through the ME joint constraint for these close pairs)

The result is **over-confident posteriors near data points** — the evidence from close neighbours is effectively counted more than once.

### When HBME IS approximately valid

The double-counting is negligible when the two data sets are **informationally independent**:

$$I(X_0;\, \text{S\_mcp}) \approx 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{S\_mcp is fully decorrelated from } X_0$$

This happens only when `dmax_mcp` lies **entirely beyond the correlation range** `a`. But then:
- Data in S_mcp → all decorrelated → MCP prior → `p(c)` everywhere (the original problem)

There is a fundamental tension:

```
dmax_mcp << a  →  MCP uses correlated data  →  informative prior
                                              →  but data leakage (double counting)

dmax_mcp >> a  →  MCP uses decorrelated data →  prior = global marginal (flat)
                                              →  no data leakage, but uninformative
```

There is **no clean operating point** that simultaneously gives an informative, spatially varying prior AND avoids data leakage.

### A rigorous alternative: annular MCP prior

One way to make HBME more sound is to compute the MCP prior from data in the **ring between the two radii** — i.e., data in `S_bme \ S_mcp` (outside the local BME zone, inside a larger zone):

```python
# Use only data OUTSIDE the local BME zone for the MCP prior
mask_ring = (dist_to_ck > dmax_bme) & (dist_to_ck <= dmax_outer)
cs_ring = cs[mask_ring, :]
ps_ring = ps[mask_ring, :]

pk_mcp_prior = MCPcatPdf(ck0, cs_ring, ps_ring, ...)  # only ring data
# BME uses close data: dmax_bme
pk_final = BMEcatPdf(ck0, cs, ps, ..., prior=pk_mcp_prior, dmax=dmax_bme)
```

This separates the data used for the prior from the data used in the likelihood. However, if `dmax_outer` is much larger than `a`, the ring data is again decorrelated → prior degenerates to `p(c)`.

### Summary comparison

| Approach | Data independence | Spatial variation in prior | Mathematical rigour |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BMEcatPdf`, uniform prior | ✓ perfect (no prior data) | ✗ flat (global marginal fallback far from data) | ✓ sound |
| HBME, `dmax_mcp < a` | ✗ data leakage (S_mcp in both steps) | ✓ yes, if data is within range | ✗ not strictly sound |
| HBME, `dmax_mcp > a` | ✓ approximately independent | ✗ degenerates to p(c) | ✓ approximately sound but uninformative |
| **XGBoost prior (BMEpriorPDF)** | **✓ perfect** (covariates ≠ spatial obs) | **✓ yes, full spatial variation** | **✓ rigorously Bayesian** |

**Conclusion:** The HBME limited-buffer approach is a practical approximation, not a mathematically rigorous Bayesian update. It works heuristically but double-counts correlated evidence. The `BMEpriorPDF` from XGBoost — passed as the Bayes-factor-corrected prior `q(c)/p(c)` — is the rigorous solution to the problem you are trying to solve: a spatially varying, informative prior derived from data that is independent of the spatial category observations.

## Finding: No Data Exclusion in the Current HBME Code

Searching the current `HBMEcatPdf` (lines 1878–1912): the MCP step uses **all** of `cs`/`ps` within `dmax_mcp`, and the BME step immediately after uses **all** of `cs`/`ps` within `dmax`. There is **zero exclusion** of MCP-range data from the BME step.

The **only** exclusion in `BMEcatPdf` (lines 1451–1459) handles the exact-collocated case (`d = 0`) — that is a different mechanism entirely.

So the data-leakage issue is **real and unaddressed** in the current code. The user's intuition about exclusion is a good idea to add.

## A Unified Mathematical Framework

### The Bayes Factor for any prior

As established, `L_ME(c)` already carries an implicit `p(c)` weight. The correct posterior with any informative prior `q(c)` is:

$$p_\text{post}(c) \;\propto\; \underbrace{\frac{q(c)}{p(c)}}_{\text{Bayes factor}} \cdot L_\text{ME}(c)$$

This works for both sources of prior:

| Prior source | `q(c)` | Bayes factor `q(c)/p(c)` |
|---|---|---|
| XGBoost / BMEpriorPDF | Covariate-based prediction | Non-uniform if covariates predict something different from global average |
| MCP (annular zone) | MCP estimate from ring data | Non-uniform if ring data is correlated; → uniform if beyond range (safe) |
| Global marginal (no extra info) | `p(c)` | ≡ 1 → no effect (correct default) |

### Solving data leakage for MCP: the annular approach

To avoid reusing data, the MCP prior should be computed from data in the **ring** between the two radii:

```
|------ dmax_inner ------|--------- dmax_mcp ---------|
 BME uses this zone only   MCP uses this ring zone only
```

This gives strict Bayesian independence between prior data and likelihood data.

## Proposed Implementation

The changes span two functions. Here are the complete proposed replacements (switch to Agent mode to apply):

### 1. Updated `BMEcatPdf` — accept Bayes-factor-corrected prior

The key addition is a `'global_marginal'` option. When provided, any `prior_pdf_at_ck` is treated as a raw probability `q(c)` and the Bayes factor `q(c)/p(c)` is computed automatically before entering `producttablepdf`.

```python
def BMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options=None):
    # ... (keep all existing docstring and options handling unchanged up to line ~1410) ...

    # ── NEW: Bayes-factor correction ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # 'global_marginal': array (nc,) of empirical category frequencies p(c).
    # When provided, any supplied prior_pdf_at_ck is treated as a raw
    # probability q(c), and the Bayes factor q(c)/p(c) is computed
    # automatically so that the ME prior's implicit p(c) weight is cancelled
    # and replaced by q(c) without double-counting.
    global_marginal = options.get('global_marginal', None)
    apply_bayes_factor = (global_marginal is not None) and (external_priors is not None)
    if global_marginal is not None:
        global_marginal = np.asarray(global_marginal, dtype=float).ravel()
        # Protect against zero entries
        global_marginal = np.clip(global_marginal, 1e-15, None)
        global_marginal /= global_marginal.sum()
    # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    pk = np.ones((nk, ncat)) * np.nan
    for i in range(nk):
        ck0 = ck[[i], :]
        cslocal, pslocal, ds, sumnslocal, _ = neighbours(
            ck0, cs, ps, nsmax, dmax, options=options)

        # ── determine prior_to_use (existing logic, unchanged) ───────────────
        if has_array_of_priors:
            prior_to_use = external_priors[i, :]
        elif external_priors is not None:
            prior_to_use = external_priors
        elif options.get('use_neighbor_average_as_prior', False) and sumnslocal > 0:
            prior_to_use = np.mean(pslocal, axis=0)
        else:
            prior_to_use = uniform_prior
        prior_to_use = prior_to_use.flatten()

        # ── NEW: apply Bayes-factor correction ───────────────────────────────
        if apply_bayes_factor:
            # q(c) / p(c) — replace the ME prior's implicit p(c) with q(c)
            bayes_factor = prior_to_use / global_marginal
            bayes_factor = np.clip(bayes_factor, 1e-15, None)
            bayes_factor /= bayes_factor.sum()   # normalise so weights sum to 1
            prior_to_use = bayes_factor
        # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        # ... rest of the loop (maxentropytable, producttablepdf, etc.) unchanged ...
```

### 2. Updated `HBMEcatPdf` — annular MCP + Bayes factor

```python
def HBMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options=None):
    """
    Performs Hybrid BME (HBME) categorical data prediction.

    Two-step approach:
    1. **Regional prior (MCP step, annular zone):**  MCPcatPdf is run on data
       in the ring  dmax < r <= dmax_mcp  (strictly outside the BME zone).
       This eliminates data leakage: the prior data and likelihood data are
       disjoint sets.  A Bayes-factor correction q(c)/p(c) is applied so that
       BMEcatPdf's implicit p(c) assumption is not double-counted.
    2. **Local update (BME step):**  BMEcatPdf uses the nsmax closest neighbours
       within dmax, with the Bayes-factor-corrected MCP prior.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ...
    options : dict, optional
        - 'nsmax_total' (int): Max neighbours in the MCP annular ring. Default 20.
        - 'dmax_mcp' (float): Outer radius of the MCP ring. Must be > dmax.
          Defaults to 2 * dmax.  Set to the covariance correlation range or
          slightly beyond.
        - 'use_annular_mcp' (bool): If True (default), restrict MCP to the ring
          dmax < r <= dmax_mcp, ensuring strict data independence.
          If False, use ALL data within dmax_mcp (original behaviour, faster
          but has data leakage).
        - 'global_marginal' (array, nc): Empirical category frequencies p(c).
          Required for the Bayes-factor correction.  If None, estimated
          automatically from ps.mean(axis=0).
        - All other options forwarded to BMEcatPdf.
    """
    if options is None:
        options = {}

    bme_options  = options.copy()
    mcp_options  = options.copy()

    nsmax_total    = bme_options.pop('nsmax_total', 20)
    mcp_options.pop('nsmax_total', None)
    dmax_mcp       = bme_options.pop('dmax_mcp', 2.0 * dmax)
    mcp_options.pop('dmax_mcp', None)
    use_annular    = bme_options.pop('use_annular_mcp', True)
    mcp_options.pop('use_annular_mcp', None)

    # ── Determine global marginal p(c) for Bayes-factor correction ────────────
    gm = options.get('global_marginal', None)
    if gm is None:
        gm = ps.mean(axis=0).astype(float)          # empirical from soft data
    gm = np.clip(gm, 1e-15, None)
    gm /= gm.sum()
    # Inject into BME step so it can apply the correction
    bme_options['global_marginal'] = gm
    # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    bme_options['model_structure'] = 'full'
    bme_options['show_progress']   = 0
    mcp_options['show_progress']   = 0

    show_progress = options.get('show_progress', 0)
    nk   = len(ck)
    ncat = Pmodel.shape[0]
    pk   = np.ones((nk, ncat)) * np.nan

    for i in range(nk):
        ck0 = ck[[i], :]

        # ── Step 1: Compute MCP prior from the annular ring ───────────────────
        if use_annular:
            # Keep only data OUTSIDE the local BME zone → strict independence
            from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist as _cdist
            dist_all = _cdist(ck0, cs).ravel()
            ring_mask = (dist_all > dmax) & (dist_all <= dmax_mcp)
            cs_ring   = cs[ring_mask, :]
            ps_ring   = ps[ring_mask, :]
        else:
            # Original behaviour: use all data within dmax_mcp
            cs_ring  = cs
            ps_ring  = ps

        if cs_ring.shape[0] == 0:
            # No ring data → fall back to global marginal as prior
            pk_mcp_prior = gm[np.newaxis, :]
        else:
            pk_mcp_prior = MCPcatPdf(
                ck0, cs_ring, ps_ring, dmodel, Pmodel,
                nsmax_total, dmax_mcp, options=mcp_options
            )
        # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        # ── Step 2: BME update with Bayes-factor-corrected MCP prior ─────────
        # Pass raw q(c); BMEcatPdf will compute q(c)/p(c) internally because
        # 'global_marginal' is set in bme_options.
        bme_options['prior_pdf_at_ck'] = pk_mcp_prior   # shape (1, nc)

        pk_final = BMEcatPdf(
            ck0, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel,
            nsmax, dmax, options=bme_options
        )
        pk[i, :] = pk_final

        if show_progress == 1:
            print(f'HBME: {i+1}/{nk}')

    return pk
```

### 3. Using `BMEpriorPDF` (XGBoost) — no code change needed

With the updated `BMEcatPdf`, using an XGBoost prior is simply:

```python
# xgb_prior shape: (nk, nc)  — from your BMEpriorPDF function
global_marginal = ps.mean(axis=0)   # or fit separately

bme_options = {
    **base_options,
    'prior_pdf_at_ck': xgb_prior,       # raw q(c) from XGBoost
    'global_marginal' : global_marginal, # triggers Bayes-factor correction
}
pk_xgb = BMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options=bme_options)
```

## What Each Design Decision Achieves

```
Scenario                   prior_to_use in producttablepdf   Posterior far from data
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Default (no options)        1/nc  (uniform)                   p(c)  ← correct
Prior = p(c), no BF         p(c)                              p(c)² ← double count ✗
Prior = q(c), no BF         q(c)                              q(c)·p(c) ← partial  ✗
Prior = q(c), with BF       q(c)/p(c)                         q(c)  ← correct      ✓
MCP annular, with BF        q_mcp(c)/p(c)                     q_mcp(c) ← correct   ✓
```

The `global_marginal` option acts as the **key**: when absent, `BMEcatPdf` behaves exactly as before (backward compatible). When present, every supplied prior is automatically Bayes-factor-corrected, regardless of whether it came from MCP or XGBoost.

## What was changed and why

### `BMEcatPdf` — two additions

**1. New `global_marginal` option in docstring** (before `Returns`)  
Documents that the option is **silently ignored when no prior is given**, making the backward-compatibility guarantee explicit.

**2. Bayes-factor setup block** (after `external_priors` validation, before the main loop):
```python
_global_marginal = None
if external_priors is not None:          # ← guard: only active with a prior
    _gm_raw = options.get('global_marginal', None)
    if _gm_raw is not None:
        _global_marginal = np.clip(np.asarray(_gm_raw).ravel(), 1e-15, None)
        _global_marginal /= _global_marginal.sum()
```

**3. Bayes-factor application inside the loop** (after `prior_to_use = prior_to_use.flatten()`):
```python
if _global_marginal is not None:
    _bf = prior_to_use / _global_marginal   # q(c)/p(c)
    prior_to_use = np.clip(_bf, 1e-15, None)
    prior_to_use /= prior_to_use.sum()
```

**Behaviour matrix:**

| `prior_pdf_at_ck` | `global_marginal` | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Not set (default) | Any | Original BME, no change |
| Set to `q(c)` | Not set | `q(c)` used directly (old behaviour) |
| Set to `q(c)` | Set to `p(c)` | `q(c)/p(c)` used — Bayes-factor corrected ✓ |

---

### `HBMEcatPdf` — three additions

**1. New `use_annular_mcp` option** (default `True`)  
Filters the MCP data set to the ring `dmax < r <= dmax_mcp` so that MCP and BME never share data. Set to `False` to recover the original all-data behaviour.

**2. Auto-estimated `global_marginal`**  
`p(c)` is computed from `ps.mean(axis=0)` (or taken from `options` if the caller already computed it), then injected into `bme_options['global_marginal']`. This ensures the Bayes-factor correction is **always active for HBME** without any extra caller work.

**3. Ring-filtered `MCPcatPdf` call**  
```python
_ring_mask = (dist > dmax) & (dist <= dmax_mcp)
cs_mcp, ps_mcp = cs[_ring_mask], ps[_ring_mask]
# falls back to global marginal if ring is empty
```

---

### How to use with an XGBoost prior

No changes to `BMEcatPdf`'s API are needed — just supply both keys in `options`:

```python
# xgb_prior: (nk, nc) array from your BMEpriorPDF / XGBoost model
global_marginal = ps.mean(axis=0)   # or fit separately

pk_xgb = BMEcatPdf(ck, cs, ps, dmodel, Pmodel, nsmax, dmax, options={
    **base_options,
    'prior_pdf_at_ck' : xgb_prior,         # q(c) from XGBoost
    'global_marginal'  : global_marginal,   # triggers Bayes-factor correction
})
```

---

## Changes made

### `BMEcatPdf` — 3 edits

**1. `prior_pdf_at_ck` docstring** — now clearly states the correction is automatic:
> *When this option is set, the Bayes-factor correction is applied automatically. `p(c)` is estimated from `ps.mean(axis=0)` unless overridden via `'global_marginal'`.*

**2. `global_marginal` docstring** — simplified to "optional override":
> *Optional override for `p(c)`. If not provided, `p(c)` is estimated automatically from `ps.mean(axis=0)`. Ignored when `'prior_pdf_at_ck'` is `None`.*

**3. Bayes-factor setup block** — now always activates when a prior is given:
```python
_global_marginal = None
if external_priors is not None:          # prior supplied → correction is ON
    _gm_raw = options.get('global_marginal', None)
    if _gm_raw is not None:
        _global_marginal = np.asarray(_gm_raw, ...).ravel()   # caller override
    else:
        _global_marginal = ps.mean(axis=0).astype(float).ravel()  # auto
    _global_marginal = np.clip(_global_marginal, 1e-15, None)
    _global_marginal /= _global_marginal.sum()
```

Now I have the exact MCP formula. Let me derive the answer rigorously from the implementation.

---

## The MCP Formula (from the code)

In log-space, the MCP posterior for category \(c_0\) given \(n\) neighbours is (lines 1763–1791):

$$\log p_\text{MCP}(c_0) = \underbrace{(1-n)\log P(c_0)}_{\text{prior correction}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{n} \log\!\left[\sum_{c_k} P(c_k,\, c_0)\cdot p_\text{data}(c_k)\right]}_{\text{likelihood sum}} + \text{const}$$

The `(1-n)` factor is the critical prior-correction term. Let's trace what happens to each out-of-range point.

---

## What Happens to Out-of-Range Data: Exact Derivation

**Outside the correlation range**, the bivariate table factorises:

$$P(c_k, c_0) \;\approx\; P(c_k)\cdot P(c_0)$$

So each out-of-range likelihood term becomes:

$$\sum_{c_k} P(c_k,\, c_0)\cdot p_\text{data}(c_k) \;\approx\; P(c_0)\cdot \underbrace{\sum_{c_k} P(c_k)\cdot p_\text{data}(c_k)}_{A_k \;\text{(constant, no }c_0\text{)}}$$

Taking the log: $\;\log[\cdots] \approx \log P(c_0) + \log A_k$

Now substitute for the full dataset with \(n_\text{in}\) in-range and \(n_\text{out}\) out-of-range points:

$$\log p_\text{MCP}(c_0) = (1 - n_\text{in} - n_\text{out})\log P(c_0) + \sum_{k\in\text{in}} \log[\cdots]_k + \sum_{j\in\text{out}} \bigl(\log P(c_0) + \log A_j\bigr)$$

$$= \underbrace{(1 - n_\text{in})\log P(c_0)}_{\text{correct prior correction for in-range only}} + \sum_{k\in\text{in}} \log[\cdots]_k + \underbrace{\sum_j \log A_j}_{\text{constant, cancels in normalisation}}$$

**This is mathematically identical to running MCP with only the \(n_\text{in}\) in-range data points.** The out-of-range contributions exactly cancel after normalization.

### Your intuition is theoretically correct — **but only under ideal conditions**.

---

## The Two Sources of Contamination in Practice

### 1. Imperfect factorisation near the range boundary

The bivariate table is never *exactly* $P(c_k)P(c_0)$ at finite distance — it approaches that only asymptotically. At distances equal to the nominal "correlation range" (e.g. where $C(h)/C(0) = 0.05$ for an exponential model), there is still 5% residual correlation. Each such point contributes a small residual signal:

$$\sum_{c_k} P(c_k,c_0)\cdot p_\text{data}(c_k) = P(c_0)\cdot A_k + \underbrace{\text{small residual term}}_{\propto \text{residual cov}}$$

The residual biases the estimate slightly toward the distribution of the out-of-range data. Including many such points accumulates these small biases.

### 2. The `nsmax` quota problem (the more dangerous issue)

The `neighbours` function returns the **closest** `nsmax` points within `dmax`. If `dmax` is huge but `nsmax` is small, you get the `nsmax` closest points — those are the most informative ones. **This case is safe.**

But if `dmax` is large and there are many near-range points exceeding `nsmax`, the function still returns only the closest `nsmax` — so large `dmax` with finite `nsmax` is actually just controlled by `nsmax`. **Also safe.**

The problem only arises in a different scenario: **if you use `nsmax` much larger than the number of correlated data points.** Then the "quota" fills with uncorrelated far data:

| `nsmax` relative to in-range data | Effect |
|---|---|
| `nsmax` ≈ `n_in` | Only in-range data used — ideal |
| `nsmax` >> `n_in` | Fills up with far data — approximate cancellation, small contamination |
| `nsmax` >> `n_in`, soft data has strong spatial trend | More contamination; far data may have different category distribution |

---

## Concrete Numerical Example

Say the global marginal is $P = [0.5, 0.5]$, and you have 2 in-range points that strongly suggest category 1 (local $p_\text{data} \approx [0.9, 0.1]$) and 10 out-of-range points from a different zone where $p_\text{data} \approx [0.1, 0.9]$.

Under **perfect** factorisation, the 10 out-of-range points cancel and MCP correctly returns a strong preference for category 1.

Under **realistic** factorisation (5% residual), each out-of-range point contributes $\approx 0.05$ "vote" toward category 2. With 10 such points, that's equivalent to 0.5 in-range votes pulling toward category 2 — potentially overwhelming the 2 genuine in-range signals.

---

## Summary and Practical Recommendations

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Can you set `dmax` very large?** | **Yes, if `nsmax` is set close to the expected number of in-range data points.** Large `dmax` with small `nsmax` is safe because `neighbours` always returns the closest `nsmax` points. |
| **Will out-of-range data cancel exactly?** | **No — only approximately.** The closer to the range boundary, the stronger the residual contamination. |
| **Does including too many out-of-range points contaminate?** | **Yes, gradually.** Contamination scales with `n_out × residual_correlation`. If the out-of-range zone has a different category distribution from the estimation location, the contamination pushes the estimate toward that zone. |
| **Best practice** | Set `dmax` ≈ correlation range and `nsmax` ≈ expected number of points within that radius. This gives the annular zone control used in `HBMEcatPdf`. |

The annular design in the updated `HBMEcatPdf` (`use_annular_mcp=True`) precisely implements the theoretically clean choice: only data that cannot cancel out (i.e. data genuinely inside the correlation range but outside the BME local zone) is used for the MCP prior, so you get the spatial trend signal without either the double-counting or the imperfect-cancellation contamination.
